items.title: Acute Effects of Impella 5.5 on Biventricular Filling and Pressure-Volume Area in Patients With Heart Failure Associated Cardiogenic Shock.
items.abstract: Use of Impella 5.5 in patients with decompensated heart failure-associated cardiogenic shock (ADHF-CS) is increasing as a bridge to advanced therapies. The effects of maximal trans-valvular unloading on biventricular filling and pressure-volume area (PVA) in ADHF-CS are poorly understood. Nine patients with medically refractory ADHF-CS underwent Impella 5.5 placement with simultaneous invasive arterial, venous, and biventricular pressure-volume loop analysis. Acutely after Impella 5.5 activation, cardiac output (3.4 ± 0.5 vs. 5.0 ± 0.7 L/min, p = 0.0011), diastolic (67.2 ± 8.0 vs. 80.7 ± 9.7 mm Hg, p = 0.0044) and mean arterial pressures (77.9 ± 7.1 vs. 86.9 ± 10.4 mm Hg, p = 0.029) increased, compared to baseline. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (24.1 ± 6.7 vs. 16.8 ± 5.4 mm Hg, p = 0.0027), volume (262.1 ± 103.9 vs. 231.5 ± 104.3 ml, p = 0.0036), and PVA (21,913 ± 7,055 vs. 18,357 ± 7,758 mmHg·ml, p = 0.013) decreased. Right ventricular end-diastolic (12.4 ± 4.6 vs. 9.1 ± 3.8 mm Hg, p = 3.8E-5) and end-systolic pressure (42.1 ± 11.9 vs. 34.4 ± 11.1 mm Hg, p = 0.030) and PVA (6,303 ± 3,851 vs. 4,437 ± 2,473 mm Hg·ml, p = 0.027) also decreased. These findings suggest that maximal left ventricular unloading can acutely reduce biventricular filling pressures and PVA in patients with ADHF-CS.

items.title: Impact of Thoracotomy-Based Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation on Right Ventricular Functional Preservation.
items.abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction remains a critical determinant of outcomes following left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation. We used a doubly robust inverse probability weighting based on propensity scores to evaluate the association between surgical approach and clinical outcomes in 187 consecutive patients (thoracotomy: n = 55; sternotomy: n = 132). The primary endpoint was RV systolic function in the early postoperative period, assessed by tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE). Despite comparable baseline RV performance and hemodynamics, the thoracotomy-based approach was associated with superior preservation of postoperative RV systolic function compared to median sternotomy (TAPSE: 12.0 vs. 11.0 mm, p = 0.001). In weighted regression models, median sternotomy was associated with a significant reduction in postoperative TAPSE (β = -0.085, p = 0.036) and a 35% relative increase in hospital length of stay (p = 0.015). Furthermore, accounting for heart transplantation as a competing risk, median sternotomy was associated with a significantly higher hazard of long-term mortality (subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR]: 1.78, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.07-3.00, p = 0.027). These findings suggest that the clinical benefits of sternal-sparing techniques extend beyond acute functional protection. This surgical strategy supports the use of less invasive approaches to optimize both early recovery and long-term outcomes in the LVAD population.

items.title: Development and Validation of a Blood Test Informed Risk Prediction Model for Lung Cancer-The Copenhagen Lung Cancer Risk Model (CPH-Lung).
items.abstract: Lung cancer screening reduces lung cancer mortality, but identifying high-risk individuals remains difficult. We wanted to develop a blood test-based risk model (CPH-Lung) to improve risk stratification before image-based screening. We included individuals from two prospective general population cohorts to model 6-year lung cancer risk; the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS) for training and the Copenhagen City Heart Study (CCHS) for validation. We analyzed clinical and biochemical variables from ever-smokers (689 cases and 1,924 controls) nested within CGPS to train a 6-year lung cancer risk model. CPH-Lung was validated in a cohort of ever-smokers age ≥50 years in the Copenhagen City Heart Study (CCHS, 3,195 individuals) and compared with the validated PLCOm2012 model. There were 689 and 68 events of 6-year lung cancer in the CGPS and the CCHS. In the CCHS validation study, the CPH-Lung versus the PLCOm2012 yielded AUCs of 0.783 (95% CI, 0.731 to 0.835) versus 0.720 (95% CI, 0.669 to 0.770) for detection of all 6-year lung cancers ( P = .0059). The discrimination was similar in the CGPS. At specificity of 77.7% (as would have been achieved using currently applied screening criteria, eg, NELSON or NLST), sensitivities were 57.6% versus 39.2% in women ( P P = .004) for CPH-Lung versus PLCOm2012. The mean age at diagnosis was 68.2 years (standard deviation [SD], 7.50) in the 120 individuals with lung cancer predicted exclusively by CPH-Lung compared with 76.5 years (SD, 8.04) in the 37 individuals predicted exclusively by PLCOm2012 ( P < .0001). After inclusion of blood test information, the CPH-Lung model was more sensitive in the Danish population than PLCOm2012 for prediction of 6-year lung cancer risk particularly among women and younger individuals.

items.title: Beyond the Average Patient: The Ergodicity Problem in Evidence-Based Medicine and a Proposal for Individual-Dynamic Medicine.
items.abstract: Evidence-based medicine (EBM) replaced authority with appraisal and has reduced harm. Its own methodologists have documented a persistent gap between what its methods conclude and what its practice does: average effects that are marginal for most treated patients, guidelines that misfit the individual, widespread difficulty converting relative into absolute effects, and no built-in trigger for stopping a treatment that is not helping. To identify a common source of these problems in the application of population-level estimates to individuals, and to propose a framework that corrects it without abandoning controlled evidence. Conceptual and critical analysis drawing on the methodological critique of EBM published by its founders and leading epidemiologists; the theory of ergodicity in dynamical systems and its empirical tests; the reference class problem; and existing clinical existence proofs of individual-level measurement and closed-loop intervention. The assumption that a population estimate applies to an individual is the ergodic assumption, which holds when a process is homogeneous across persons and stationary over time. Homogeneity fails whenever treatment response differs between people, which is common; where an individual's responses are reproducible, individual-level inference is both necessary and feasible. Large within-person variability weakens every inference and must be measured rather than assumed away. The N-of-1 randomised trial, which estimates an effect in the individual, was published by Guyatt and Sackett in 1986 and ranks at Level 1 of the Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence, yet a systematic review found 108 published trials in twenty-five years. I propose Individual-Dynamic Medicine, a biocybernetic framework of six principles, each with an existence proof in mainstream medicine, specifying how population evidence and within-person trials divide the work of an individual decision, and state its assumptions, limitations, and the predictions on which it could fail. Modern medicine decides which treatments work by testing them on large groups and averaging the results. That answers one question well: does this treatment help a population? But doctors treat one person at a time, and a group average can say surprisingly little about any one member of the group. A treatment that “works” may need to be given to four people, or fifty, for one to benefit on the outcome measured, and whether that means a few people respond strongly or everyone responds a little cannot be told from the trial. A method for testing a treatment in a single patient has existed since 1986 and sits at the top of the profession's own evidence ranking, yet it is rarely used. This paper explains why the group average fails as a guide to the individual, using arguments the founders of evidence‐based medicine themselves published, and proposes a practical framework in which the individual patient, measured over time, becomes the unit of evidence. The tools are already in use in diabetes care, pain research, and cardiology. The paper also states what would have to be true for the proposal to be wrong.

items.title: Advances in photothermal therapy for antibacterial biomedical materials: Photothermal agents, near-infrared windows, and combination strategies.
items.abstract: Bacterial infections, particularly those involving multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections in wound and implant-related settings, remain difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics alone. Photothermal therapy (PTT) has emerged as a non-antibiotic antibacterial strategy owing to its localized heat generation, broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, spatial controllability, and low risk of inducing conventional drug resistance. The antibacterial efficacy of PTT is largely governed by photothermal agents (PTAs), whose light absorption capacity, photothermal conversion efficiency, structural stability, biosafety, and bacterial interfacial interactions determine therapeutic performance. This review summarizes recent advances in antibacterial PTT from the perspectives of PTA design, excitation windows, and therapeutic integration. Representative first near-infrared window (NIR-I) PTAs, including noble metal nanomaterials, carbon-based nanomaterials, metal sulfides/oxides, metal-organic frameworks, and organic PTAs, are discussed with emphasis on their structural characteristics, photothermal mechanisms, surface regulation strategies, and antibacterial performance. Recent progress in second near-infrared window (NIR-II) PTAs is then highlighted, particularly their advantages in deeper tissue penetration, biofilm treatment, imaging-guided therapy, and precise intervention in complex infections. PTT-based combination strategies involving photodynamic therapy, chemodynamic therapy, and immunotherapy are also reviewed to illustrate how localized heat can synergize with oxidative damage, catalytic radical generation, immune modulation, and infection microenvironment regulation to enhance antibacterial efficacy. Finally, challenges and future directions of antibacterial PTT are discussed, including improving PTA stability and biocompatibility, minimizing thermal damage to normal tissues, enhancing infection-site responsiveness, and promoting clinical translation. Overall, this review provides a materials and biointerface perspective on how PTA design, NIR excitation, and therapeutic integration can guide the development of effective antibacterial photothermal platforms and their clinical translation.

items.title: Influenza Vaccination Preferences Among Adults Aged 60 Years and Older in Beijing, China.
items.abstract: Influenza vaccination coverage among older adults remains suboptimal in China despite free vaccination policies in some regions. Understanding their preferences may inform strategies to improve uptake. To quantify preferences for influenza vaccination attributes and assess preference heterogeneity by prior influenza vaccination history. This community-based survey study was conducted at 2 districts in Beijing, China, where influenza vaccination is provided free of charge for adults aged 60 years or older. A convenience sample of adults aged 60 years or older was included from 6 Beijing subdistricts and participated in a discrete choice experiment conducted from August to September 2025. Stated choice among 2 hypothetical influenza vaccination profiles and an opt-out option. Attributes included vaccine effectiveness, risk of mild adverse effects, vaccination venue and operating hours, outreach method, information source, and message content. Conditional logit, mixed logit, scenario simulations, and vaccination-history interaction analyses were performed. Among 514 participants included in the analyses, the median age was 71 years (IQR, 65-79 years), and 356 (69.3%) were women. Higher vaccine effectiveness was associated with greater vaccination preference (β = 2.12; 95% CI, 1.37 to 2.88), whereas higher perceived risk of mild adverse effects was associated with lower preference (β = -5.53; 95% CI, -7.83 to -3.22). Participants preferred community-based vaccination settings, telephone reminders (β = 1.06; 95% CI, 0.76 to 1.36), information from government or community organizations (β = 0.78; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.02), and messages emphasizing protection of family members (β = 0.50; 95% CI, 0.26 to 0.74). Increasing vaccine effectiveness from 20% to 80% and reducing perceived risk of adverse effects from 20% to 5% were associated with 30.74- and 19.96-percentage-point (pp) increases in the model-estimated choice probability, respectively. Compared with participants with prior vaccination, never-vaccinated participants had a greater preference for opting out (difference in β = 1.07; 95% CI, 0.11 to 2.03), greater sensitivity to mild adverse effect risk (difference in β per 10-pp increase, -0.49; 95% CI, -0.93 to -0.05), and lower responsiveness to vaccine effectiveness (difference in β per 10-pp increase, -0.18; 95% CI, -0.31 to -0.04). In this discrete choice experiment of older adults in Beijing, influenza vaccination preferences were associated with vaccine profiles, trusted communication, and community-based service delivery. Prior vaccination history identified differences in benefit-risk weighting that may inform broad and targeted vaccination strategies.

items.title: Cross database bibliometric and knowledge mapping analysis of nanoplatform mediated tumor associated macrophage reprogramming.
items.abstract: Nanoplatforms are evolving from passive delivery vehicles into multifunctional engineered systems capable of remodeling the tumor microenvironment. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are important biological interfaces because of their abundance, plasticity, and roles in immune suppression and therapeutic resistance. However, the knowledge structure and developmental trajectory of nanoplatform-mediated TAM reprogramming remain insufficiently characterized. We performed a bibliometric and knowledge-mapping analysis using independently retrieved Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus datasets with cross-database comparison and consistency assessment. English-language articles and reviews published from January 1, 2007, to March 25, 2026, were included, yielding 1,474 WoSCC and 2,077 Scopus records. Analyses used bibliometrix, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, BiblioVista, and Scimago Graphica. Publication output increased markedly in both databases, particularly after 2019, with highly concordant annual trends (Spearman's ρ = 0.996, p < 0.001). The field was primarily represented in nanoscience, materials science, pharmacology, biomaterials, and biomedical engineering. China and the Chinese Academy of Sciences were the leading country and institution, while ACS Nano and Journal of Controlled Release formed the principal journal core. Keyword, burst, thematic, and milestone analyses supported a heuristic five-stage transition from macrophage-addressable nanodelivery to material-intrinsic immunomodulation, microenvironment-responsive TAM reprogramming, biomimetic and combinatorial nano-immunotherapy, and programmable innate-immunity-centered nanoplatforms. Translation-related themes remained comparatively less visible. Nanoplatform-mediated TAM reprogramming has developed into a rapidly expanding interdisciplinary research area linking nanoplatform engineering, macrophage-directed regulation, and tumor microenvironment remodeling. Future advancement will likely depend on increasingly sophisticated platforms alongside improved reproducibility, standardization, predictable in vivo behavior, and clinical translatability.

items.title: Immunotherapy for oral cavity tumors: recent advances, key challenges, and future perspectives.
items.abstract: Oral cavity tumors remain a major global health challenge, with poor outcomes in patients with locally advanced, recurrent, or metastatic disease despite advances in surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies. Immunotherapy has emerged as a potential strategy to restore antitumor immunity and overcome tumor-induced immune suppression. This narrative review synthesizes recent advances in immunotherapy for oral cavity tumors, focusing on immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) antibodies, near-infrared photoimmunotherapy (NIR-PIT), bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), oncolytic viruses (OVs), cytokine therapies, and adoptive cell therapies such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T/natural killer (NK), and T cell receptor (TCR)-T therapy. The review also examines the pivotal role of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) in shaping treatment response and therapeutic resistance, highlighting the contributions of regulatory immune cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), hypoxia, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and immune exclusion. Current clinical evidence demonstrates meaningful survival benefits with programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitors in recurrent/metastatic disease and expanding opportunities for perioperative immunotherapy, while numerous emerging modalities remain under active clinical investigation. However, durable responses remain limited by tumor heterogeneity, inadequate immune cell trafficking, antigen escape, manufacturing challenges, and the lack of reliable predictive biomarkers. Future progress will likely depend on biomarker-guided patient selection, rational combination strategies, and engineered cellular therapies that can overcome microenvironment-mediated resistance. Collectively, these findings support continued investigation of personalized, multimodal immunotherapy as a viable avenue for improving outcomes in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

items.title: A three-step serum-free protocol for the robust generation of monocyte-derived dendritic cells from human hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells.
items.abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) and their monocyte precursors are rare in peripheral blood, which limits their use in immunotherapy. Although hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) provide an alternative source, they are even less abundant in vivo. To address this limitation and compensate for apoptosis during the generation of DCs from monocytes, we developed a three-step serum-free protocol (culture system) that combines HSPC expansion with sequential differentiation. The protocol comprises a 7-day HSPC expansion phase, a 14-day monocyte induction phase, and a 7-day DC generation phase-5 days of differentiation followed by 2 days of maturation with either tumor necrosis factor-α or lipopolysaccharide. Cell quantification revealed that the system generated approximately 5,000 monocytes and 50 DCs from a single HSPC. The generated DCs expressed the key surface markers CD40 and CD209 and exhibited antigen uptake capacity comparable to that of native CD14⁺ monocyte-derived DCs. Overall, this system provides a reproducible and scalable platform for studying DC biology and supports applications in preclinical and translational immunotherapy research.

items.title: Predictors of immunological non-response despite virological suppression in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Immunological Nonresponse (INR) in people living with HIV (PLWH) is characterized by inadequate CD4+ T-cell recovery despite effective viral suppression through antiretroviral therapy (ART). This systematic review and meta-analysis identify key clinical, demographic, and molecular predictors of INR to optimize immune recovery strategies. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, yielding 59 eligible studies, with a total of 19,511 individuals with INR. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), and pooled effect estimates were calculated as odds ratio (OR), mean difference (MD), or standardized mean difference (SMD). Significant predictors of INR included male sex [OR 1.33 (1.12-1.58)], older age [MD 2.61 (1.42-3.81)], intravenous drug use [OR 1.67 (1.15-2.42)], hepatitis B coinfection [OR 1.30 (1.08-1.57)], hepatitis C coinfection [OR 1.85 (1.50-2.28)], tuberculosis [OR 1.77 (1.41-2.21)], advanced HIV stage [OR 2.66 (2.34-3.02)], and lower baseline and nadir CD4+ counts [SMD -3.82 (-4.94-(-2.70)), SMD -1.69 (-2.69-(-0.68))], respectively. Additionally, 57 biomarkers were identified as potential predictors of INR, implicating several immunological pathways. These findings underscore the multifactorial nature of INR and the need for personalized approaches among ART-treated individuals.

items.title: Structural and biochemical insights into HCV envelope proteins for germline-targeting vaccines.
items.abstract: Despite effective antivirals, Hepatitis C remains a global health burden, reflecting the difficulty of eliciting broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs). For the Hepatitis C virus, bnAb responses are biased toward VH1-69-encoded Abs targeting a conserved epitope on the E2 glycoprotein, suggesting that effective immunogens must engage the corresponding germline (GL) B cell receptors. However, the structural basis of GL recognition remains unclear. Here, we show that GL-reverted VH1-69 bnAbs recognize the E2 core domain in a manner closely resembling mature Abs binding. High-resolution structures reveal a conserved mode of engagement, indicating that key epitope features are accessible prior to affinity maturation. Guided by these insights, we engineered E2 variants to enhance GL Ab interactions and stability. Although these designs increased affinity, they did not improve engagement of naïve B cells, highlighting a key constraint in GL-targeting strategies. Together, our findings define principles governing GL recognition and inform the rational design of an HCV vaccine.

items.title: Harm reduction services in female prisons: a scoping review exploring the situation in the MENA region.
items.abstract: This study aims to explore and map the existing evidence on HR services, specifically NSP and OST, available to women in prison settings across MENA countries where such services are reported to exist, assessing their availability, accessibility, and gender responsiveness while identifying gaps in research, policy, and practice. Harm reduction (HR) is a public health and human rights approach aimed at reducing drug-related harms through interventions such as Opioid Substitution Therapy (OST) and needle and syringe programs (NSPs). People who use drugs (PWUDs) in prison face elevated risks of HIV, Hepatitis B and C, Tuberculosis and overdose. Women who use drugs (WWUDs) experience additional gender-specific vulnerabilities, yet little is known about its availability and gender responsiveness of prison-based HR in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Full-text peer-reviewed and grey literature published, in English, between 2014 and 2024 were retrieved from PubMed, Cochrane Library, JSTOR, Google Scholar and key organizational reports. Studies addressing NSP and/or OST in prison settings within MENA countries were included. Data were synthesized narratively focusing on service availability, accessibility and gender responsiveness. Of 4,238 records identified, 27 studies met inclusion criteria (14 peer-reviewed articles and 13 grey literature sources). Evidence was concentrated in Iran, with limited data from Afghanistan, Morocco and Lebanon, and none from Algeria. OST was reported in several prison settings, while NSP was limited to Iran. Most studies lacked sex-disaggregated data, and where women were included, they were frequently underrepresented and rarely analyzed separately. Evidence on gender-responsive services, post-release care and monitoring and evaluation systems was limited. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study provides the first regional synthesis of evidence on gender-responsive HR services for WWUD in MENA prisons, identifying substantial gaps in service provision, gender-disaggregated evidence and evaluation.

items.title: Identification of Host Interaction Partners of the Hepatitis E Virus Internal Ribosome Entry Site-Like RNA Using RNA-Protein Interaction Detection Assay and Yeast Three-Hybrid Assay.
items.abstract: Internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) are structured RNA elements that facilitate cap-independent translation initiation. IRES activity is regulated by its interactions with host and viral RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), collectively known as IRES trans-acting factors (ITAFs), which modulate RNA folding, ribosome recruitment, and translation efficiency. Characterizing these RNA--protein interactions provides valuable insights into the mechanisms that regulate IRES activity. Hepatitis E virus (HEV), is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus. Our earlier study discovered an IRES-like (IRESl) element in the genotype 1-HEV (g1-HEV), which mediated translation of the open reading frame four (ORF4). This chapter describes our stepwise protocol to identify host proteins that associate with the HEV-IRESl using two independent methods: the yeast three-hybrid (Y3H) assay and the RNA-protein interaction detection (RaPID) assay. The Y3H assay enables genetic screening of host cDNA libraries to identify RBPs that bind to an RNA sequence in vivo, while the RaPID assay employs proximity-dependent biotinylation to capture transient interactions in mammalian cells. Together, these methods offer a robust approach for identifying the dynamic network of IRES-associated RBPs.

items.title: Machine learning-driven SERS fingerprinting for high-accuracy serum screening of hepatic inflammation in mice.
items.abstract: Hepatitis screening is clinically challenging. Conventional serological and biochemical assays rely on cumbersome procedures, require long detection times, and lack sufficient sensitivity to identify pathological changes. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) enables rapid, label-free, and high-sensitivity molecular fingerprinting of biological fluids. It holds great promise for noninvasive serum biochemical analysis. Here, we report a machine learning-enhanced SERS platform based on a sugar-cube-like Ag nanocrystal (SC-AgN) substrate for accurate discrimination between healthy and DMN-induced hepatitis mouse serum. We fabricated the SC-AgN substrate with favourable uniformity, reproducibility and SERS enhancement to capture robust and well-resolved spectra from mouse serum samples. Clear spectral differences were identified in hepatitis serum, which correspond to protein denaturation, lipid peroxidation, and disturbed nucleic acid metabolism. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to reduce dimensionality, remove spectral noise, and eliminate redundant spectral features. The optimized spectral variables were further imported into a sparse partial least-squares discriminant analysis (SPLS-DA) model for precise sample classification. The finalized PCA-SPLS-DA model achieved an accuracy of 96.7%, a sensitivity of 100.0%, a specificity of 94.6%, and an AUC of 0.973 (95% CI, 0.945-0.992) for distinguishing DMN-induced hepatitis from healthy serum samples. This diagnostic performance outperforms that of conventional spectroscopic approaches. This work establishes a robust SC-AgN-based SERS diagnostic strategy integrated with the PCA-SPLS-DA model, which is expected to provide a rapid, low-cost and high-accuracy solution for hepatitis screening and auxiliary clinical diagnosis.
items.journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications

items.title: Novel Tool to Predict Primary Tumor Location in the Setting of Metastatic Cancer With Unknown Primary.
items.abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate a tool to predict the primary tumor site in patients with metastatic cancer of unknown primary using demographic and clinical variables, including imaging-derived sites of metastasis, without pathology or laboratory data. In this population-based study, data were extracted from the SEER database. Patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2020 with a known primary cancer site, metastatic staging, and metastasis in the bone, liver, brain, and lungs were included. Patients were randomly split into training (70%) and/or testing (30%) sets. A total of 27 primary tumor sites were included. A gradient boosting model was trained to predict the primary tumor site, with random forest and classification tree models evaluated as comparators. Random guess and frequency-weighted guessing models were used for baseline comparison. A total of 689,715 patients were included from 9,208,295 queried. The most common primary cancer sites were non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (n = 211,338), intestines (n = 64,187), and pancreas (n = 60,310). The baseline models achieved Top-5 accuracies of 0.179 for a random guess and 0.476 for a frequency-weighted guess. The gradient boosting model achieved Top-1, Top-3, and Top-5 accuracies of 0.40 ± 0.001, 0.680 ± 0.001, and 0.790 ± 0.001, respectively, across 100 Monte-Carlo replicates. Top-5 accuracy was highest for primary NSCLC (0.990 ± 0.001) and intestinal cancer (0.900 ± 0.003). Our model was most influenced by sex (gain = 0.27) and metastasis to bone (gain = 0.20). A web app was constructed: primarycancerpredictor.netlify.app. This study developed and evaluated a gradient boosting machine learning model and a user-friendly web tool to aid in the diagnosis of cancer of unknown primary.

items.title: Adapting Segment Anything Model 3 for concept-driven lesion segmentation in medical images: an experimental study.
items.abstract: Accurate segmentation of lesions is fundamental for medical image analysis. However, most existing approaches are designed for specific anatomical sites and imaging modalities, limiting their applicability in heterogeneous clinical environments. Recent vision-language foundation models have enabled concept-driven segmentation of natural images, offering a promising path toward more flexible and generalizable medical image segmentation. However, to the best of the authors' knowledge, concept-prompt-based lesion segmentation in medical images, particularly using the latest Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3), has not been thoroughly examined. In this paper, the authors present a systematic investigation of the SAM3 framework for lesion segmentation. An extensive evaluation of SAM3 was first conducted using geometric bounding boxes and concept-based text and image exemplars as prompts for lesion segmentation across multiple cancer types and imaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, ultrasound, dermoscopy, and endoscopic imaging, with particular emphasis on volumetric medical imaging datasets. To improve robustness and segmentation accuracy, additional knowledge into the input representation was further integrated, including predictions from adjacent slices, multiparametric imaging information, and prior annotations. In addition, the study compared different SAM3 fine-tuning strategies on the BraTS2023-MET dataset, including partial module fine-tuning, adapter-based optimization, and full-model fine-tuning, under different training objectives. Extensive experiments conducted on 13 datasets covering 11 lesion types demonstrate that SAM3 achieves strong cross-modality generalization and accurate instance-specific lesion delineation. These results highlight the potential of concept-driven foundation models for scalable and practical medical-image segmentation in real-world clinical settings. The source code and dataset splits are publicly available at https://github.com/apple1986/lesion-sam3 .

items.title: Suppressor with morphogenetic effect on genitalia 7 (SMG7) drives hepatocellular carcinoma progression through context-dependent nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) dysregulation.
items.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet the molecular mechanisms linking metabolic stress to tumor progression remain poorly defined. RNA surveillance pathways, including nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), may represent a relevant but unexplored regulatory layer in this context. In this study, we analyzed the expression of NMD components across multiple human HCC and MASLD cohorts, identifying suppressor with morphogenetic effect on genitalia 7 (SMG7) as a key regulator of NMD associated with HCC progression. In vitro functional assays, NMD target expression, transcriptomic profiling, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) were used to identify downstream pathways and mediators. More than 40% of NMD components were dysregulated in HCC. Among them, SMG7 was consistently upregulated across HCC and MASLD cohorts, induced by lipotoxic stress, and identified as a hub gene in HCC transcriptional networks. SMG7 overexpression promoted proliferation, migration, and clonogenicity, whereas its silencing reduced tumor aggressiveness in a context-dependent manner inversely associated with UPF1 levels. Combined depletion of SMG7 and UPF1 suppressed aggressive traits in vitro and limited tumor growth in vivo. Transcriptomic and network analyses identified Z-DNA-binding protein 1 (ZBP1) as a downstream mediator of SMG7 dysregulation in SNU-387 HCC cells, a finding further supported by functional rescue experiments. These results identify the SMG7-ZBP1 axis as a metabolic stress-responsive pathway linking NMD dysfunction to liver tumor progression and highlight NMD modulation as a therapeutic strategy to restrain tumor aggressiveness while enhancing tumor immunogenicity.

items.title: Comparative toxicity and efficacy of consolidative thoracic radiotherapy after first-line chemoimmunotherapy in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer: real-world retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: First-line chemoimmunotherapy (CT-IT) is the standard treatment for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), while consolidative thoracic radiotherapy (cTRT) may improve local control and survival. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of cTRT after first-line CT-IT in patients with ES-SCLC in a real-world setting. This retrospective cohort study included 199 patients with ES-SCLC who received first-line CT-IT. Patients were divided into a CT-IT + cTRT group (n = 97) and a CT-IT alone group (n = 102). Survival outcomes included progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). Treatment-related adverse events were assessed. The two groups were generally comparable at baseline, although the CT-IT + cTRT group had fewer brain metastases and more favorable response-related features after induction treatment. Median PFS and OS were significantly longer in the CT-IT + cTRT group (both P < 0.001). cTRT (P < 0.001) and a longer duration of maintenance immunotherapy (P = 0.031) were independently associated with a better PFS. For OS, cTRT was associated with better survival status (P = 0.003) and liver metastasis with poorer survival status (P = 0.015). Regarding safety, grade 1-2 dermatitis and gastrointestinal toxicity were more frequent in the CT-IT + cTRT group, whereas rates of pneumonitis, esophagitis, immune-related adverse events, and grade 3-4 toxicities were comparable between groups. In this real-world retrospective cohort, the addition of cTRT to first-line CT-IT was associated with significantly improved PFS and OS in patients with ES-SCLC, without an apparent increase in severe treatment-related toxicity. Prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings and refine patient selection for cTRT.
items.journal: Strahlentherapie und Onkologie : Organ der Deutschen Rontgengesellschaft ... [et al]

items.title: Quantifying the Role of Interventional Radiology in Managing Patients with Hepatobiliary Cancers.
items.abstract: To quantify the role of interventional radiology (IR) in managing primary and secondary hepatobiliary cancers. This retrospective study analyzed administrative data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) using final action claims for Medicare Fee-for-Service beneficiaries from 2016 to 2021. Patients aged ≥65 years with hepatobiliary cancer were identified using International Classification of Diseases (ICD), 10th Revision, codes. Services and associated work Relative Value Units (wRVUs) provided by IR, medical oncology, radiation oncology, and surgical oncology were identified using CMS physician specialty codes. IR procedures were classified as therapeutic or supportive. From 2016 to 2021, the Medicare hepatobiliary cancer cohort included 108,317-111,761 patients annually (mean age, 75 years; male, 53%). Medical oncologists treated 70% of patients, followed by interventional radiologists with 51%, radiation oncologists with 13%, and surgical oncologists with 5%. Physician service volumes and wRVU remained stable, with medical oncologists providing the largest share (69% of services and 13.7% of wRVUs), followed by interventional radiologists (2.9% and 11.7%, respectively), radiation oncologists (1.3% and 4.5%, respectively), and surgical oncologists (0.1% and 2.2%, respectively). Interventional radiologists performed 75,785 therapeutic procedures, primarily for hepatocellular carcinoma (59%). Before pandemic, IR volumes increased 57%, driven by liver ablations (+25%) and supportive services (+63%), whereas transarterial therapies declined slightly (-6%). Despite the drop in volume during the pandemic, IR saw the highest compound annual growth rate (4%) among the specialties analyzed. IR provides a substantial share of services for patients with hepatobiliary cancers, with rising use of therapeutic and supportive services, delivering similar wRVUs at lower costs, underscoring its growing role in cancer care.
